clinicalPearls: Distal intersection syndrome is a tenosynovitis occurring where the extensor pollicis longus crosses over the extensor carpi radialis longus and brevis, distal to Lister's tubercle.
It is much less common and more distal than the classic proximal intersection syndrome, which occurs where the first-compartment muscles cross the radial wrist extensors.
Pain, swelling and sometimes crepitus localise to the dorsal wrist around Lister's tubercle rather than the more proximal forearm.
The extensor pollicis longus is at risk because it angulates sharply around Lister's tubercle, where friction and tenosynovitis can precede attritional rupture.
Ultrasound or MRI shows peritendinous oedema and fluid at the crossover point of the extensor pollicis longus with the radial wrist extensors.
First-line management is activity modification, splinting and anti-inflammatory measures, with corticosteroid injection used cautiously given the rupture risk.
It must be distinguished from de Quervain tenosynovitis, isolated extensor pollicis longus tenosynovitis and dorsal wrist ganglion.
reference.pathophysiology: At the dorsal wrist the extensor pollicis longus turns sharply around Lister's tubercle and crosses superficial to the second-compartment radial wrist extensors, the extensor carpi radialis longus and brevis. Repetitive wrist and thumb motion generates friction at this distal crossover, producing a peritendinous tenosynovitis with oedema and, at times, crepitus. Persistent inflammation combined with the sharp angulation of the tendon around the tubercle can compromise the extensor pollicis longus and predispose it to attritional rupture, analogous to the rupture seen after distal radius fracture.
additionalDifferentials: Extensor pollicis longus tenosynovitis or impending rupture
Scapholunate pathology or dorsal wrist impingement
Second carpometacarpal or carpal boss pathology
additionalInvestigations: Ultrasound demonstrating peritendinous fluid at the extensor pollicis longus crossover
MRI showing oedema and tenosynovitis at the crossover distal to Lister's tubercle
Plain radiographs to exclude bony causes and prior distal radius fracture
Clinical Finkelstein test to help differentiate de Quervain tenosynovitis
Dynamic assessment for crepitus on wrist and thumb motion
redFlags: Signs of impending or actual extensor pollicis longus rupture, such as loss of thumb retropulsion
History of distal radius fracture with new dorsal wrist pain
Failure to respond to appropriate conservative care
Rapidly progressive swelling suggesting infection or inflammatory arthropathy
reference.prognosis: The condition is usually self-limiting and responds well to conservative measures, though delayed recognition risks extensor pollicis longus attrition and rupture.
pitfalls: Confusing it with the more common proximal intersection syndrome or de Quervain tenosynovitis.
Injecting corticosteroid carelessly and risking extensor pollicis longus rupture.
Missing an impending tendon rupture, especially after distal radius fracture.
Mislocalising the pathology proximally in the forearm.
references: Rockwood and Green's Fractures in Adults
management: Modify activity with relative rest from repetitive wrist and thumb motion
Apply wrist and thumb splinting to offload the extensor pollicis longus at Lister's tubercle
Use ice and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory measures for peritendinous inflammation
Give any corticosteroid injection cautiously because of the risk of attritional extensor pollicis longus rupture
Monitor vigilantly for impending or actual extensor pollicis longus rupture with prompt hand-surgery referral
Undertake surgical decompression and tenosynovectomy, with tendon transfer or reconstruction if rupture occurs
Provide physiotherapy and ergonomic or technique correction before return to activity
